bibl.title: Testing multi-scale processing in the auditory system

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: How the auditory system integrates sound over time - whether on one continuous timescale or on two distinct ones.
span.quote: Integrating information over time, as we define it operationally here, serves as a basic information accumulation process in the auditory system to guarantee that enough information is supplied for extracting meaningful regularities on a certain timescale.

span.label: Natural sound carries information on several timescales at once - does one integration process handle all of them, or are there separate windows for detail and for pattern?
span.quote: Therefore, by hypothesis, a single integration process may not suffice for the variety of auditory tasks that the system successfully solves.

span.label: Shows that performance on fine detail does not improve with longer stimuli - which the older integration models predict it should - and supports two concurrent temporal windows instead.
span.quote: Behavioral task performance that requires processing fine-detail information does not improve with longer stimulus length, contrary to predictions of previous temporal integration models such as the multiple-looks and the spectro-temporal excitation pattern model.

span.label: mechanism
span.quote: Here we use a paradigm requiring processing on relatively ‘local’ and ‘global’ scales and provide evidence suggesting that the auditory system extracts fine-detail acoustic information using short temporal windows and uses long temporal windows to abstract global acoustic patterns.

span.label: auditory temporal integration across timescales
span.quote: The temporal integration of sound is a fundamental property of hearing.

span.label: behavioural-experiment
span.quote: Here, to explore mechanisms of temporal integration and test certain predictions of the different integration models, we investigated in a series of four psychophysical experiments the perceptual performance at shorter and longer scales by manipulating the timescale of acoustic information while biasing the auditory processes implementing local or global task demands.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: sampled acoustic information is passed to a second, representational stage of limited capacity, so what reaches perception is not the full set of samples
span.quote: In a second stage, the sampled information is channeled to a representational stage with limited information capacity and probably with a time constant of hundreds of milliseconds.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: when too much detail is squeezed into that limited-capacity representation the system smooths or summarises it, destroying the local detail that the task requires
span.quote: However, the limited information capacity of the representation stage forces the auditory system to smooth or summarize all information.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: inserting gaps lowers the amount of information per unit time, letting local detail be represented precisely
span.quote: After intervals are inserted between segments, information per unit time decreases, so local details can be represented in a more precise manner.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: stretching a stimulus with gaps pushes segments outside the single long temporal window, so the global pattern can no longer be sampled
span.quote: As the long temporal window is around hundreds of milliseconds, inserting intervals stretches the stimuli and makes few segments fall within one long temporal window, so a global pattern of the stretched stimuli cannot be sampled.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: two windows run concurrently: about 30 ms for parsing acoustic structure at high resolution, about 200 ms for extracting the global pattern
span.quote: one temporal window, of ~30 ms or less in which acoustic structure is parsed and analyzed with relatively high temporal resolution; and another temporal window of ~200 ms in which acoustic information is extracted at a more global scale

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: the two models are separated by a prediction, not by plausibility: more stimulus should mean better detail discrimination under multiple-looks and STEP, and need not under 2TWI
span.quote: In contrast, the 2TWI model suggests that increased stimulus length may not necessarily increase performance, because representation and processing of local details might function best only at a time range of tens of milliseconds 29 , 32 .

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: the older account is leaky integration with a time constant of hundreds of milliseconds, under which performance rises with duration and plateaus above 200 ms
span.quote: Previous models of temporal integration typically assume leaky integration with a time constant of hundreds of milliseconds, based on studies such as loudness summation 15 , 16 , signal detection in noise 17 , 18 , and temporal integration at threshold 13 , 19 , 20 , 21 , 22 , in which listeners’ performance increases continuously with sound duration and typically achieves a plateau above 200 ms.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: multiple-looks resolves the paradox by sampling fast and concatenating - so the long timescale is BUILT from short samples rather than being independent
span.quote: The multiple-looks model suggests that temporal integration is a process of multiple timescales instead of one, but the longer timescale is assembled on the basis of concatenated short samples.

span.label: At short (15-20 ms) and long (50-100 ms) segment durations the local-task data may be at floor or ceiling, so the effect of stimulus length could not be observed there.
span.quote: Therefore, the effect of increased stimulus length cannot be observed probably because of a ceiling effect.

span.label: Responses from the same-different paradigm were analysed as if from a yes-no paradigm, and participants may have adopted a differencing strategy.
span.quote: Participants in our experiments may adapt a “differencing” strategy as in the same-different task, since there is no obvious perceptual token in our stimuli as well as stimuli of different segment durations and stimulus lengths were grouped and presented randomly in each task.

span.label: Experiment 3A gives a result opposite in direction to Experiment 1B on segment number, attributed post hoc to fixing the first and last segments.
span.quote: We suspect that the discrepancy is caused by the fact that we fixed the first and the last segments in Experiment 3A, so differences between two stimuli within the ‘different’ pair are much smaller in 3-segment stimuli (only one segment is different) than in 5-segment stimuli (three segments are different).

span.label: The literature it enters is thin - the multi-scale process itself is described as not widely investigated.
span.quote: However, this multi-scale process in the auditory system is not widely investigated in the literature, and existing models of temporal integration are mainly built upon detection or recognition tasks on a single timescale.

span.label: The two-window sizes carry a physiological commitment the psychophysics alone cannot establish.
span.quote: These findings support the hypothesis of a dual-scale processing likely implemented in the auditory cortex.

span.label: The design is borrowed from existing local-global paradigms rather than built for the question.
span.quote: Our approach is conceptually analogous to previous local-global studies 39 , 40 .

span.label: a separate experiment (Experiment 4) varying the inter-stimulus interval systematically, with d-prime found not to vary across ISIs
span.quote: Although memory requirements may come into play in our experiment due to the characteristics of the same-different procedure, the results of this control experiment demonstrate that memory cannot explain the main results obtained in the previous experiments.

span.label: integration - as a single leaky accumulator with one time constant, under which more sound always means better performance
span.quote: Previous models of temporal integration typically assume leaky integration with a time constant of hundreds of milliseconds, based on studies such as loudness summation 15 , 16 , signal detection in noise 17 , 18 , and temporal integration at threshold 13 , 19 , 20 , 21 , 22 , in which listeners’ performance increases continuously with sound duration and typically achieves a plateau above 200 ms.

span.label: integration - as fast discrete sampling then concatenation, where the long scale is assembled from short samples
span.quote: The multiple-looks model suggests that temporal integration is a process of multiple timescales instead of one, but the longer timescale is assembled on the basis of concatenated short samples.

span.label: integration - as two independent concurrent windows, where the long scale is not built from the short one and each does its own job
span.quote: In contrast, the 2TWI model suggests that increased stimulus length may not necessarily increase performance, because representation and processing of local details might function best only at a time range of tens of milliseconds 29 , 32 .

span.label: contradicts → the multiple-looks model (Viemeister) and the spectro-temporal excitation pattern (STEP) model (Moore)
span.quote: However, we find that the performance of discrimination between two stimuli with different fine-grained information decreases, which is inconsistent with the prediction of a multiple-looks model and a STEP model.

span.label: builds-on → the multiple-looks and STEP models
span.quote: Inspired by the multiple-looks and STEP models, we suggest a slightly different temporal integration process to account for the present results.

span.label: replicates → McDermott et al. and Piazza et al.
span.quote: The results of Experiment 1 are consistent with recent findings by McDermott et al . 46 and Piazza et al . 47 , who also showed that increased stimulus length helps the auditory system perceive global statistical patterns but can impede access to local acoustic detail.

span.label: extends → Poeppel (2001, 2003) multi-time resolution hypothesis for speech
span.quote: Such a multi-time resolution hypothesis, proposed by Poeppel (2001, 2003) for speech is probably a general mechanism for audition, not just a specific model for speech perception as was originally argued.

span.label: contradicts → the multiple-looks and spectro-temporal excitation pattern models
span.quote: Behavioral task performance that requires processing fine-detail information does not improve with longer stimulus length, contrary to predictions of previous temporal integration models such as the multiple-looks and the spectro-temporal excitation pattern model.

span.label: builds-on → the two-temporal-windows integration model
span.quote: Although the two-temporal-windows integration model (2TWI) shares some basic features with the multiple-looks and STEP models, there are significant differences, as well.

span.label: extends → previous local-global paradigms
span.quote: Our approach is conceptually analogous to previous local-global studies 39 , 40 .

span.label: multiple-looks —contrasted-with→ leaky integration
span.quote: The multiple-looks model suggests that temporal integration is a process of multiple timescales instead of one, but the longer timescale is assembled on the basis of concatenated short samples.

span.label: resolution-integration paradox —causes→ multiple-looks
span.quote: To resolve this paradox, Viemeister (1991) proposed a ‘multiple-looks’ model: the continuous sound is sampled discretely at a high rate (e.g. with integration windows of ~5 ms), and the samples are stored and concatenated/integrated for further processing.

span.label: temporal window —part-of→ temporal integration
span.quote: one temporal window, of ~30 ms or less in which acoustic structure is parsed and analyzed with relatively high temporal resolution; and another temporal window of ~200 ms in which acoustic information is extracted at a more global scale

span.label: d-prime (sensitivity index)
span.quote: Responses were transformed into the sensitivity index, d prime, and criterion, denoted as C, as in a simple yes-no paradigm using the Palamedes toolbox 44 .

span.label: ANOVA
span.quote: A two-way repeated measures ANOVA with the factors task and segment duration was conducted at each level of stimulus length, followed by a one-way repeated measures ANOVA to evaluate the main effect of segment duration within each task at each level of stimulus length.

span.label: two-alternative forced choice d-prime
span.quote: In Experiment 2, we used a two-interval two-alternative-forced choice paradigm and d prime values were computed accordingly.

span.label: Making a sound longer improved listeners' ability to judge its overall global pattern but did not improve their ability to compare its fine acoustic detail.
span.quote: However, longer stimuli only improved integration in a global task , but did not increase performance on extracting fine-grained information in a local task .

span.label: Lengthening the individual segments had the opposite effect from lengthening the whole stimulus: it helped the local task and hurt the global task.
span.quote: Furthermore, increasing segment duration increases participants’ performance in the local task but decreases the performance in the global task .

span.label: With longer stimuli listeners shifted their decision criterion, increasingly calling two genuinely different sounds 'the same'.
span.quote: Furthermore, in Experiment 1B, the criterion in the local task increased with stimulus length, which indicates that subjects became worse at analyzing local details and tended to consider two sounds in the ‘different’ pair to be the same.

span.label: Inserting silent gaps between segments raised sensitivity in the local task while lowering it in the global task.
span.quote: Figure 3b shows that d prime value s increased as the IOIs increased in the local task (Experiment 3A) but decreased in the global task (Experiment 3B).

span.label: Varying the silent interval between the two sounds of a pair from 500 to 1500 ms left performance unchanged, so memory decay cannot explain the stimulus-length effect.
span.quote: Figure 4 illustrates that d prime value s did not change across different ISIs for a given stimulus length.

span.label: Global frequency-trend discrimination still improved with stimulus length when the onset and offset frequency differences were equated, ruling out a simple spectral-edge cue.
span.quote: Figure 2b summarizes the results: as the number of segments (i.e. stimulus length) increased, d prime value s increased.

span.label: The local-task result contradicts the multiple-looks and STEP models, which predict better discrimination of fine detail as more samples become available.
span.quote: The performance on the local task shows that differentiating sounds based on detailed, local spectrotemporal information does not increase with increasing stimulus length.

span.label: Holding the number of segments constant while stretching the stimulus with gaps made performance better, not worse, so working-memory load does not drive the effect.
span.quote: The results from Experiment 3A also demonstrate that the working memory load cannot explain the effect of stimulus length in the local task of Experiment 1.

span.label: The pattern replicates earlier reports that longer sounds aid global statistical perception while blocking access to local acoustic detail.
span.quote: The results of Experiment 1 are consistent with recent findings by McDermott et al . 46 and Piazza et al . 47 , who also showed that increased stimulus length helps the auditory system perceive global statistical patterns but can impede access to local acoustic detail.

span.label: Fine-detail performance does not improve with longer stimuli - the prediction that separates the old models from the new one fails for the old ones.
span.quote: Behavioral task performance that requires processing fine-detail information does not improve with longer stimulus length, contrary to predictions of previous temporal integration models such as the multiple-looks and the spectro-temporal excitation pattern model.

span.label: Hearing a sound as one unitary event takes more than hundreds of milliseconds.
span.quote: Moreover, the perceptual construction of putatively ‘unitary’ auditory events requires more than hundreds of milliseconds.

span.label: The field's two bodies of evidence conflict: integration studies plateau above 200 ms, resolution studies find thresholds of 2-30 ms.
span.quote: In those studies, perceptual thresholds from 2–30 ms are the norm.

span.label: The timescales are not arbitrary - speech carries phonemic, syllabic and intonational information at three separate ranges.
span.quote: For example, speech conveys linguistic information at several scales: 20–80 ms for phonemic information, 100–300 ms for syllabic information, and more than 1000 ms for intonation information 1 .

span.label: temporal integration (operational definition)
span.quote: Integrating information over time, as we define it operationally here, serves as a basic information accumulation process in the auditory system to guarantee that enough information is supplied for extracting meaningful regularities on a certain timescale.

span.label: inter-onset interval (IOI)
span.quote: The IOI is defined here as the duration between the onset of one segment and the onset of the next segment (see Fig. 3a ).

span.label: local task
span.quote: In the local task , the sweep directions of each corresponding segment were the same between two stimuli in the ‘same’ pair, whereas the sweep directions of each corresponding segment in the ‘different’ pair were opposite.

span.label: temporal integration, operationally
span.quote: Integrating information over time, as we define it operationally here, serves as a basic information accumulation process in the auditory system to guarantee that enough information is supplied for extracting meaningful regularities on a certain timescale.

span.label: the multiple-looks model
span.quote: To resolve this paradox, Viemeister (1991) proposed a ‘multiple-looks’ model: the continuous sound is sampled discretely at a high rate (e.g. with integration windows of ~5 ms), and the samples are stored and concatenated/integrated for further processing.

span.label: the resolution-integration paradox
span.quote: This incompatibility has led to the formulation of the resolution-integration paradox 8 , 26 .

span.label: the two temporal windows
span.quote: one temporal window, of ~30 ms or less in which acoustic structure is parsed and analyzed with relatively high temporal resolution; and another temporal window of ~200 ms in which acoustic information is extracted at a more global scale

span.label: stimulus length
span.quote: In Experiment 1A, two factors, stimulus length and segment duration , were manipulated.

span.label: segment duration
span.quote: In Experiment 1A, two factors, stimulus length and segment duration , were manipulated.

span.label: inter-stimulus interval (ISI)
span.quote: The factors, segment number (i.e. overall stimulus length) and inter-stimulus interval (ISI), were manipulated.

span.label: d prime sensitivity in the same-different judgement
span.term: d prime sensitivity in the same-different judgement
span.quote: Responses were transformed into the sensitivity index, d prime, and criterion, denoted as C, as in a simple yes-no paradigm using the Palamedes toolbox 44 .

span.label: working memory load
span.quote: By inserting intervals into the stimuli, we kept the working memory load constant and stretched the stimuli to make the task more memory demanding, but the participants’ performance became better rather than worse.

span.label: frequency difference between the two stimuli at onset and offset
span.term: frequency difference between the two stimuli at onset and offset
span.quote: The frequency difference between two stimuli at the onset was the same as the frequency difference at the offset, so the participants could not rely on spectral cues to judge the trend of the frequency shift.

span.label: sweep direction of corresponding segments in the global task
span.term: sweep direction of corresponding segments in the global task
span.quote: In the global task , the sweep directions of corresponding segments between two stimuli were always different because we wanted to prevent participants from making judgments based on acoustic details.

span.label: stimulus length, and whether the task demands local detail or global pattern
span.term: stimulus length, and whether the task demands local detail or global pattern
span.quote: Here, to explore mechanisms of temporal integration and test certain predictions of the different integration models, we investigated in a series of four psychophysical experiments the perceptual performance at shorter and longer scales by manipulating the timescale of acoustic information while biasing the auditory processes implementing local or global task demands.

span.label: discrimination performance on the same-different task
span.term: discrimination performance on the same-different task
span.quote: Behavioral task performance that requires processing fine-detail information does not improve with longer stimulus length, contrary to predictions of previous temporal integration models such as the multiple-looks and the spectro-temporal excitation pattern model.

span.label: 4.482 — ceiling d-prime value imposed by adding a half artificial incorrect trial to all-correct blocks
span.quote: Therefore, the maximum d-prime value for all correct responses is 4.482 (instead of infinity) and the minimum d-prime value is 0.

span.label: 1600 — trials presented in the local task of Experiment 1A, and the same number again in the global task
span.quote: In Experiment 1A, 1600 trials in total were presented in the local task and the same number in the global task .

span.label: Twenty-two — participants recruited across Experiments 1A and 1B
span.quote: Twenty-two participants, who were all right-handed and had no known hearing deficit, took part in the experiment.

span.label: ~30 ms and ~200 ms — the two integration windows proposed by the 2TWI model
span.quote: one temporal window, of ~30 ms or less in which acoustic structure is parsed and analyzed with relatively high temporal resolution; and another temporal window of ~200 ms in which acoustic information is extracted at a more global scale

span.label: 20–80 ms / 100–300 ms / >1000 ms — phonemic, syllabic and intonational timescales in speech
span.quote: For example, speech conveys linguistic information at several scales: 20–80 ms for phonemic information, 100–300 ms for syllabic information, and more than 1000 ms for intonation information 1 .

span.label: 2–30 ms — perceptual thresholds in the resolution literature - the half of the paradox the integration models cannot accommodate
span.quote: In those studies, perceptual thresholds from 2–30 ms are the norm.

span.label: 10–30 ms and 500–700 ms — the two timescales carrying information in bird song
span.quote: Bird song, similarly, also includes information on one timescale around 10–30 ms and another one around 500–700 ms 5 .
